content: reCAPTCHA is a system that leverages CAPTCHA technology to enhance the digitization of books. It works by taking scanned words that optical character recognition (OCR) software has failed to recognize and presenting them to humans for interpretation. These words are displayed as CAPTCHA challenges alongside words that the computer has already successfully identified. To ensure that humans can accurately decipher these previously unrecognizable words, the system displays two words instead of the usual single word. One of these words is a standard CAPTCHA-generated word, while the other is the undetectable word from the scanned text. If users correctly solve the standard CAPTCHA word, it is assumed that their interpretation of the undetectable word is also accurate. However, for the undetectable word to be considered definitively solved, it must be verified by multiple users. The reCAPTCHA tests are sourced from a central repository managed by the reCAPTCHA project, which supplies the undetectable words. This process is facilitated through a JavaScript API, with the server making a callback to reCAPTCHA after the user submits their response. To simplify integration, the reCAPTCHA project provides libraries for various programming languages and applications. The service is free, except for users who require an exceptionally high amount of bandwidth. The reCAPTCHA project is part of the Carnegie Mellon School of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University. It shares a similar goal with the Distributed Proofreaders project, although the latter relies on conventional human proofreaders. A press release from Carnegie Mellon University on May 24 highlighted how the project significantly contributes to book digitization efforts. Additionally, a BBC news report by Paul Rubens on October 2, 2007, described reCAPTCHA as a tool that not only combats spam but also aids in the preservation of books.
